la:adv:semper.gloss: always, ever, forever, at all times, on each occasion, ongoing, constant
senses: always, ever, forever, at all times, on each occasion, ongoing, constant
la:adv:semper.html:
semper, adv.
root sam-; Gr. ἁμ-; v. semel and -per = παρά; cf. tantisper
,
ever, always, at all times, forever (cf. usque).
In gen.: nequiter factum illud apud vos semper manebit, Cato ap. : locus hic apud nos semper liber est,: semper occant priusquam sarriunt rustici,: sat habet favitorum semper, qui recte facit,: quod improbis semper aliqui scrupus in animis haereat, semper iis ante oculos judicia et supplicia versentur: nullum autem emolumentum esse tantum, semper ut timeas, semper ut adesse, semper ut impendere aliquam poenam putes,: quod semper movetur, aeternum est,; : non haerent in suis sedibus, sed volucri semper spe rapiuntur,: curavit (Servius Tullius), quod semper in re publicā tenendum est, ne, etc.,; 3, 14, 23 et saep.: sibi exortam semper florentis Homeri Commemorat speciem (the Gr. ἀειθαλής), : hic vertex nobis semper sublimis,; cf.: quod Graeci aigleucos (ἀειγλεῦκος) vocant, hoc est semper mustum, : avida ulteriorum semper gens (semper belonging to ulter),: si umquam dubitatum est, utrum tribuni plebis vestrā an suā causā seditionum semper auctores fuerint, Drak.; for which also, without esse (hence apparently adject.): Hasdrubal pacis semper auctor,; cf.: adversus Sidicinos sumerent arma, suos semper hostes,—To strengthen the signif., joined with cottidie, perenne, assidue, etc. (as in Gr. ἀεὶ καθʼ ἡμέραν, συνεχές, etc.; v. Lidd. and Scott's Lex. under ἀει): ea mihi cottidie Aut ture aut vino aut aliqui semper supplicat,; cf. : lucrum ut perenne vobis semper suppetat,: ne semper servus currens, iratus senex, etc.... assidue agendi sint mihi,; so (with assiduus) ; : ibi semper omne vitae spatium famula fuit,: semper et ubique,; ; ; ; cf. .—
Of continuance within a definite time: ego illum antehac hominem semper sum frugi ratus,; cf. : quod tempus (aestatem) omnes Siciliae semper praetores in itineribus consumere consuerunt,: quibus studiis semper

fueris, tenemus, .—

Esp., with comp., of a progressive change (poet.): rem Romanam Alterum in lustrum meliusque semper, Proroget aevum,: candidior semper candidiorque veni,.—
Distributively, always, every time, on each occasion (ante-class. and post-Aug.): rex Creo vigiles nocturnos singulos semper locat,: horresco semper, ubi pultare hasce (fores) occipio miser,always, every time,: quattuor partus enixa, septumo semper mense, genuit, etc.,: bis inter duos exortus lunae adfluunt bisque remeant vicenis quaternisque semper horis,: tertio die cibum capere semper,: cibum capere semper diebus tertiis,.—
Transf. (poet.), everywhere, in every place (like Engl. always): proque toro terrae non semper gramen habenti, Incubat infelix,.

la:adv:semel.html:
sĕmĕl, adv. num.
root sam-, one; Sanscr. sa-, sam-, with, together; Gr. ἅμα, ἅπαξ; cf.: sem-per, sim-ilis, sim-plex, sin-gulus, etc.
.
Lit., once, a single time: ter sub armis malim vitam cernere, Quam semel modo parere, Enn. ap. Müll.; and ap. (Trag. v. 298 Vahl.); so, potin' ut semel modo huc respicias?: satis sum semel deceptus,: semel fugiendi si data est occasio, Satis est,; so, semel si, (but cf.: si semel, infra, II. B. 2 fin.): qui vel semel ita est usus oculis, ut vera cerneret, is, etc.,: ut attendant, semel bisne signum canat in castris,: semel in mense sulcos sarrito,: semel die,: in diebus,: semel anno,: in anno,: quem (Crassum) semel ait in vitā risisse Lucilius,; so, semel in vitā,: semel adhuc,: semel umquam, et saep.: M. Valerius Corvinus sellā curuli semel ac vicies sedit,; for which also: vicies et semel,: sol omni terrarum ambitu non semel major, not greater by once, i. e. not as large again, not twice as large, : haud semel sed centies,; cf. : non semel, sed bis,; : non semel, sed saepe,; : non semel sed saepius,; ; ; ; ; : non plus quam semel eloqui,; ; also without quam: plus semel, more than once, Varr. ap. : Janum Quirinum semel atque iterum clausum, once and again, i. e. twice, (for which: Janus bis clausus,; ; cf. also Plut. Num. 20); ; but also in a more gen. sense: pecuniam semel atque iterum dare coacti sunt, time and again, i. e. repeatedly, (8, 16): hoc semel ille iterumque neglexit,; cf.: cum his Aeduos semel atque iterum armis contendisse,; ; so too ; for which: semel iterumque,; : Piso saepe dicebat, minus saepe Pomponius, raro Carbo, semel aut iterum Philippus,only once or twice,; : semel et saepius,; Müll.; cf.: an quod semel jus est, idem et saepius?.—Late Lat.: semel et bis,repeatedly,; Greg. M. Ep. 5, 18 fin.—
Transf.
Pregn., like the Gr. ἅπαξ, of that which occurs no more than

once, but once, but a single time, once for all: cum facile orari, Caesar, tum semel exorari soles,: quibus semel ignotum a te esse oportet,: hostis est datus, cum quo dimicantes aut vitam semel aut ignominiam finirent,: totas semel absorbere placentas,to swallow entire cakes at once,: procubuit moriens et humum semel ore momordit,once for all,; cf.: nulla reparabilis arte Laesa pudicitia est; deperit illa semel,: semel aeternā nocte premenda fui,: nobis vero homicidio semel interdicto,once for all,: sic et semel Christus oblatus est,; Pet. 3, 18: quoniam se semel a caeli contemplatione averterunt,; hence in Florus: semel in perpetuum,: semel et in perpetuum,.—Of speech, at once, once for all, in a word, briefly: cum postulasset, ut sibi fundus, cujus emptor erat, semel indicaretur, (for which, just before: non plus quam semel): interim, quod pluribus collegit adversarius, satis est semel proponere,; cf.: ut semel, plura complectar,; ; : ut semel dicam,: ut, quod sentio, semel finiam,; cf.: quisquam denique, ut semel finiam, in lite cantat?; so (after denique) .—

In a succession = primum, primo, the first time, first: demonstravimus, L. Vibullium Rufum bis in potestatem pervenisse Caesaris, semel ad Corfinium, iterum in Hispaniā,; so after bis, with iterum, ; ; ; id. t Oud.; 72; ; after ter, with iterum and tertio, .—Without iterum, etc.: cum ad idem, unde semel profecta sunt, cuncta astra redierint,; cf.: uti exorta est semel,.—
In gen., like primum, to denote the simple antecedence of an occurrence; hence, most freq. with the particles ut, ubi, quando, cum, si, etc., once, ever, at some time, at any time: quod semel dixi, haud mutabo,what I have once said,: quod Complacitum est semel,: satis sum semel deceptus,: verebamini, ne non id facerem quod recepissem semel?: nec accidere, ut quisquam te timere incipiat eorum, qui semel a te sint liberati timore,: in id, quod semel invasit, incumbit,: retrahi nequitum, quoquo progressa est semel, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Fest. s. v. nequitum, p. 162 Müll.—So too in the comically formed proper name: Quodsemelarripides,.—With particles; with ut: in hasce aedes pedem Nemo intro tetulit, semel ut emigravimus,: ut occepi semel,: ut semel eloquentia evecta est,: ut semel gloriam consecutus sum,; : denique ut semel finiam,.—With ubi: ubi erit accubitum semel,: ubi animus semel cupiditate se devinxit malā,; ; .—With quandoquidem: perge, quandoquidem occepisti semel,.—With quando: quando in apertum semel discrimen evasura esset res,.—With cum: quae proclivius ad perniciem, cum semel coepit, labitur,.—With quoniam: (Antonius) quoniam semel induxit animum, sibi licere quod vellet, etc.,; Ov H. 12, 11: illam partem, quoniam semel ita vobis placuit, non recusabo quominus perpoliam,; ; ; .—With si: si semel amoris peculum accepit, Extemplo et ipsus periit et res,; so, si semel,: si istam semel amiseris libertatem, Brix ad loc.; : si illum semel prehendero,: si semel animum tuom perspexerit,: et semel emissum volat inrevocabile verbam, (but, semel si, if once, if ever, whenever, as an emphatic numeral, ; ; v.supra, I. init.).—With participles (several times in Liv. and Quint.): ut adversando remorandoque incitato semel militi adderent impetum, ; so ; ; ; ;

senses: a coin worth half an as
la:noun:semis.html:
sēmis, issis (in Vitr., Front., and Pall. indecl., e.g. duo semis pedes, :
duobus semis pedibus,; : diametros octo semis,: passuum milium et semis,; cf.: habere duos et semis cubitos,), m.
cf. semi-; Gr. ἡμι-, ἥμισυ
, a half, half-unity, a semi-unit (v. as, I.).
In gen. (very rare for the usual dimidium): sex domini semissem Africae possidebant,: patrimonii,: e libertorum defunctorum bonis,: cum alter semissem, alter universa fratre excluso (sibi vindicaret),: panem semissem ponebat supra torum,.—
In partic. (freq. and class.).
As a coin,
Half an as, a semi-as, Müll.; cf. P.; : lex frumentaria de semissibus et trientibus,; ; ; ; hence, non semissis homo, not worth a groat, i. e. good for nothing, worthless, Vatin. ap. a, 1: quid fit! Semis,.—
In the times of the later emperors, as a gold coin, a half aureus (containing 59.8 grains of gold, or the present value of 10s. 6 3/4d. sterling), .—
As a rate of interest, one half per cent. a month, or, acc. to our mode of computation, six per cent. a year (cf.: bes, triens, etc.): semissibus magna copia (pecuniae) est,: usura multiplicata semissibus,: usura semissium,; for which also, reversely: semisses usurarum,; and in apposition: semisses usuras promisit,; ; fin.—
As a measure of dimension.
Half a juger of land: bina jugera et semisses agri assignati,; cf. ; .—
A half-foot, half a foot: interesse sesquipedes inter bina semina in latitudinem, in longitudinem semisses,: campestris locus alte duos pedes et semissem infodiendus est,; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.; ; .—
Half a cubit: cubitum ac semissem,.—
Among mathematicians, the number three, ; cf. as fin.

la:adj:sempiternus.html:
sempĭternus, a, um, adj.
semper; like hesternus and aeternus, from heri and aevum
,
everlasting, ever-during, perpetual, continual, imperishable, eternal, sempiternal (cf. aeternus init.; very freq. and class.): fragile corpus animus sempiternus movet, etc.,; cf. : immortalis memoria et sempiterna,: deorum vita sempiterna,; cf.: aevo sempiterno frui,: ignes,; cf.: cursus stellarum,: gratias agere sempiternas,: amicus,; ; cf.: verae amicitiae,; so, hiemes,: ignis Vestae,: documentum Persarum sceleris,: memoria amicitiae nostrae,: odia,: consilium senatus,: potentia, et saep.: nihil umquam nisi sempiternum et divinum animo volutare,: nihil nisi sempiternum spectare,: in sempiternum,forever, et saep. —Adv., in three forms (not in Cic.), always, forever, perpetually. *
sempĭ-ternum, .—
sem-pĭternō, Cato ap. P.: sempiterno permanet ea materia,; ; .—
sempĭternē, Pac. ap. ; .

la:adj:semiliber.html:
sēmĭ-līber, ĕra, ĕrum, adj.,
half-free: semiliberi saltem simus,; id. ap. .

la:adj:semisomnus.html:
sēmĭ-somnus, a, um, and sēmĭ-somnis, e, adj.
somnus
,
half-asleep, sleepy, drowsy (class.): tibi siccae semisomnae,; ; Zumpt N. cr.; ; ; ; Drak.; 30, 5 fin.; 37, 20; 40, 15; ; ; : sopor, Cael. ap. : cor,.—Form semisomnis, .

la:adj:Sempronius.html:
Semprōnĭus, i, m.; Semprōnĭa, ae, f.,
the name of a Roman gens. Its most celebrated members were Ti. and C. Sempronius Gracchus, after whom are named the leges Semproniae (v. infra, A.); fem. Sempronia, wife of D. Junius Brutus, and sharer in Catiline's conspiracy, and 40, 5.—Hence,
Semprōnĭus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Sempronius: lex frumentaria,; ; : leges,; et saep.: Sempronia Horrea,a place where, by a law of C. Gracchus, the public corn was stored, Müll.; ; ; ; sqq.—
Semprō-nĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Sempronius, Sempronian: senatusconsultum,introduced by C. Sempronius Rufus,: clades,suffered by the consul C. Sempronius Atratinus,.

la:noun:semita.html:
sēmĭta, ae,f.
se-(=sed-), i.e. aside; and root mi-, to go; cf.: meo, trames
,
a narrow way, a path, foot - path, lane, by - way, etc. (opp. via, a highway; cf.: callis, trames): quā ibant, ab itu iter appellarunt; quā id anguste, semita ut semiter, dictum, Müll.
Lit. (freq. and class.): angustissimae semitae,; cf. : aut viam aut semitam monstrare,: decedam ego illi de viā, de semitā,; cf. ; : scabras lutosasque semitas spectant, id. Ira, 3, 35, 5: omnibus viis notis semitisque essedarios ex silvis emittebat,; so (opp. via) ; : semita angusta et ardua,: ut Oresti nuper prandia in semitis decumae nomine magno honori fuerunt,; ; Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 44 Vahl.): rara per occultos lucebat semita calles,: quā jacet Herculeis semita litoribus,the narrow way, et saep.—In mal. part., ; cf. vulgi, (3, 17), 1.—Prov.: qui sibi semitam non sapiunt, alteri monstrant viam, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 358 Vahl.): de viā in semitam degredi,.—
Transf., of other ways or paths (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): formicae praedam Convectant calle angusto ... opere omnis semita fervet,; so of the same,: Phryxi quā semita jungi Europamque Asiamque vetat,: spumea semita fugientis clavi,: velox Lunae pigraque Saturni,: umida Iridis,: aratri, id. de Apono, 25: arteriae, id est spiritus semitae,.—
Trop. (rare but class.), a way, path, road: locuples et speciosa vult esse eloquentia ... feratur ergo non semitis, sed campis: non uti fontes angustis fistulis colliguntur, sed ut latissimi amnes totis vallibus fluat ac sibi viam, si quando non acceperit, faciat,: illius ego semita feci viam,: jam intellegetis, hanc pecuniam, quae via modo visa est exire ab isto, eandem semita revertisse,: secretum iter et fallentis semita vitae,: semita certe Tranquillae per virtutem patet unica vitae,: novum ad victoriam iter sanguinis sui semita aperire,; so in eccl. Lat., freq., of a way of life, course of conduct, etc.: justitiae,: justorum,.

sēmēsus (sēmiēsus (trisyl.), ; and 8, 297; cf. Wagn. ), a, um, adj.
semi-edo
,
half-eaten, half-devoured, half-consumed (not ante-Aug.): praeda,: ossa,: pisces,: lardi frusta,: serpentes,: lepus,: obsonia,; : corpora liberorum,: cibi,.

sēmustus (sēmĭ-ustus), a, um, adj.
uro
,

Lit.: Enceladi semustum fulmine corpus. : robora,: facem,; ; : forum,: simulacra,; : tectorum vestigia lacera et semusta,; —
Trop.: se populare incendium priore consulatu semustum effugisse,.

la:noun:semivir.gloss: a half-man, half man and half beast, semihomo, e.g., the centaur Chiron
senses: a half-man, half man and half beast, semihomo, e.g., the centaur Chiron
a half-man in a derogatory sense of seeming effeminate or unmanly
la:noun:semivir.html:
sēmĭ-vĭr, vĭri, m.adj.,
a half-man, i. q. semihomo and semimas (not anteAug.).
Lit.
Half man and half beast, e. g. the Centaur Chiron. ; the Minotaur, (cf. semibos): Nessus,.—
An hermaphrodite, ; .—
Transf., emasculated.
Lit., of a priest of Cybele (cf. semimas), : semiviri chori,: formosum adulescentem semivirum reddidit,. —
Trop., unmanly, womanish, effeminate: et nunc ille Paris cum semiviro comitatu,: Phryx,; ; .—So esp. of debauchees: qui tam atrocem caedem pertinere ad illos semiviros crederent (for which, just before: molles and obsceni viri),: impure ac semivir,.

la:adj:semianimis.gloss: half alive, half lifeless, half dead; partly, nearly or almost dead; expiring, dying
senses: half alive, half lifeless, half dead; partly, nearly or almost dead; expiring, dying
la:adj:semianimis.html:
sēmĭ-ănĭmis (in verse, per synizesin, read as a quadrisyl.; and in some editions also written sēmănĭmis), e
anima
, and less freq. sēmĭ-ănĭmus, a, um, adj.
animus
,
half-alive, half-dead (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; syn.: semivivus, seminex).
Form semianimis: semianimes micant oculi, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 463 Vahl.): semianimesque micant digiti,; ; ; 11, 635; 12, 356; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; id. Ira, 3, 4, 3; ; ; ; —
Form semanimus (or semian-): semanimo corpore,; Cic. poët. Div. 1, 47, 106: lepus,; ; ; : corpus, Dietsch.

senses: seed (of the elements of other bodies (of fire, water, stones, etc.))
la:noun:semen.html:
sēmen, ĭnis, n.
root sa-, sē-; cf.: sero, sevi; Saturnus, sator, etc.
.
Seed.
Of plants, ; ; fin.; 34; : semen manu spargere,: terra semen excepit,; ; ; et saep.—
Of men, animals, etc., ; ; ; ; ; sq.; ; ; et saep.—
Poet., of the elements of other bodies (of fire, water, stones, etc.): ignis semina convolvunt e nubibus,; ; ; 6, 841: quaerit pars semina flammae in venis silicis,; et saep.: in animis quasi virtutum igniculi et semina,; so : alicujus quaestionis,.—
κατʼ ἐξοχήν,spelt-seed, spelt, ; ; ; cf. .—
Transf.
A shoot used for propagating; a graft, scion, set, slip, cutting, ; ; ; ; et saep.—
A stock, race (very rare): genus ac semen,; so (with genus) : ipsa regio semine orta,: videndum, ut boni seminis pecus habeas,.—
Posterity, progeny, offspring, child (poet.): non tulit in cineres labi sua Phoebus eosdem Semina, sed natum flammis Eripuit,; so, semina,; 15, 216; ; ; ; et saep.—
Trop., as in all languages, seed, i. e. origin, occasion, ground, cause; of persons, an author, prompter, insligator, etc. (class.).
Sing. (the predom. signif. in Cic.): stirps ac semen malorum omnium,: bellorum civilium semen et causa,, cf. ut in seminibus est causa arborum et stirpium: sic hujus belli semen ut fuisti (for which, just before: causam belli in personā tuā constitisse),: sceleris,.—
Plur.: in animis, quasi virtutum igniculi atque semina,: quod et Zeno in suis commentariis quasi semina quaedam sparsisset,: si virtutes sunt, ad quas nobis initia quaedam ac semina sunt concessa naturā,: loquaces, seditiosos, semina discordiarum (tribunos plebis),: vix tamen illa semina erant futurae luxuriae,the small beginnings,; cf. : discordiae,; fin.: belli,; : rebellionis,: motus,. futuri exitii, : ejus facultatis,: quamquam semina ejus (translationis) quaedam apud Aristotelen reperiuntur,: quaedam probationum,: veteris eloquentiae,; .

la:verb:semino.html:
sēmĭno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
semen
,
to sow (rare; not in Cic.; syn.: sero, planto).
Lit.: adoreum, triticum, hordeum, etc.,; ; ; 2, 9, 16: agrum,—
Transf.
To beget, engender, procreate: alter decumo post mense nascetur puer quam seminatus est,: armenta,; ; sq.—*
Of plants, to bring forth, produce: viscum quod non sua seminat arbos,.—
Trop.: cultum dei per terram,to plant, propagate, disseminate,; ; .

la:noun:semihomo.html:
sēmĭ-hŏmo, ĭnis, m.,
a half-man, i. e. half man and half beast.
Lit.: Centauri, (for which, semiferi, al.; v. semifer, I.): mandragoras (because formed below like a man), Col. poët. 10, 19.—
Trop., half-human, i. e. half-wild, half-savage, = semifer, II.: Cacus, (for which, semifer, ): Nasamones,.

la:verb:semoveo.html:
sē-mŏvĕo, mōvi, mōtum, 2, v. a.,
to move apart, to put aside, remove, separate (rare but class.; syn.: sepono, sejungo).
Lit.: vos semotae, nos soli,: qui ante voce praeconis a liberis semovebantur,.—
Trop., to part, separate, remove: Strato ab eā disciplinā omnino semovendus est,: omnes sententias eorum omnino a philosophiā,: te a curis,; for which, also: curā metuque,: egestatem ab dulci vitā,: verba,: voluptatem semovendam esse,.— Hence, sēmōtus, a, um, P. a., remote, distant, far removed.
Lit.: colloquium petunt semoto a militibus loco, * : munitiones semotarum partium, Auct. B. Alex. 2, 3: longe semota tuemur,; : terris semota,: semoti prius tarda necessitas Leti corripuit gradum,.—

the name of a Roman gens. Its most celebrated members were Ti. and C. Sempronius Gracchus, after whom are named the leges Semproniae (v. infra, A.); fem. Sempronia, wife of D. Junius Brutus, and sharer in Catiline's conspiracy, and 40, 5.—Hence,
